newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN seeks Bosnia peace with "open cities", bus rides.
newsitem.headline: UN seeks Bosnia peace with "open cities", bus rides.

text.p: With bus rides across the old frontlines and "open cities" in divided municipalities, the U.N. refugee agency is trying to break an impasse over the crisis in Bosnia with creative ways, its regional envoy said on Thursday.
Blankets and plastic sheeting were the UNHCR's staple throughout the bloody 1992-1995 war in former Yugoslavia, whose violent disintegration left Bosnia divided into ethnic ghettoes.
But now the agency is trying to overcome some of the emotional and political barriers with incentives for municipalities welcoming minorities and inter-ethnic bus rides.

Carrol Faubert, a Canadian whose official title is special envoy, told a news conference that UNHCR expects 200,000 Bosnian refugees -- among 800,000 who fled their country -- to return home this year. Last year, 250,000 went home.
But he said most would be "easy" returnees to majority ethnic areas.
"This pool will be gradually exhausted as we get towards the end of summer," Faubert said.
"Particularly on minority returns, we are now in a situation of blockage. If we want larger numbers to return, we have to achieve a breakthrough on minority returns."

To try to get over the impasse, UNHCR is promoting an "open cities" project under which ethnically tolerant municipalities will be offered financial assistance to help repair buildings, train workers and back agriculture and business, Faubert said.

He said UNHCR also operates buses that transport some 11,000 people every week across the ethnic frontlines so they can exercise their right to freedom of movement, a central feature of the 1995 Dayton peace accord that ended the war.
Many ordinary Bosnians at grass root level are more tolerant than their top leaders, Faubert said, describing some of the senior politicians as "political dinosaurs".
UNHCR has received proposals so far for 25 municipalities and two initial beneficiaries will be named next week, he said.
Among the criteria for selection are willingness to set up a joint police force and joint administration, access to services for minority groups and cooperation between leaders, he said.
Any municipality that misbehaves will be dropped, he added.
One would be the divided municipality of Gornji Vakuf in central Bosnia, where the once feuding Bosnian and Croatian authorities have started working together to rebuild the city.
UNHCR has also commissioned television programmes to try to get over some of the war wounds.
In one such programme, it linked two lovers separated by the war, a Bosnian Serb man and Bosnian Croat woman, by live satellite and broadcast their contact on local television.
Nationalist authorities in Bosnia, in violation of Dayton, have blocked refugees from rival ethnic groups from returning.
Faubert expressed frustration at the slow progress and at the international pressure to follow rigid Dayton timetables, but said he was optimistic in the medium term.
"To think that Dayton would be implemented within one year was an illusion. To think that its civilian aspects will be implemented in the next two years is another illusion," he said.

"It is clear that some of the parties to this agreement show no intention of applying the provisions. But there is progress. By the end of 1998, there should be...either a solution or at least indications or progress towards a solution."
